newsitem.title: USA: Durable goods orders post sharp Jan rise.
newsitem.headline: Durable goods orders post sharp Jan rise.

text.p: New orders for costly manufactured items increased sharply in January, the Commerce Department said on Thursday, largely on a rebound in demand for communications equipment and for electronic components.

Total orders for durable goods -- items designed to last three years or more -- shot up 3.6 percent after back-to-back drops of 1.8 percent in December and 1.7 percent in November, the department said.
The January rise in durables orders was more than twice the 1.5 percent pickup that Wall Street economists had forecast.

"It was certainly stronger than what was expected, and I think what's important is you're seeing strength excluding both the defence and transportation categories," said Kevin Flanagan, of Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

"This isn't a one-time deal where you're seeing a large order hitting the books and we can go back to a negative column. It's reinforcing the notion of a solid growth setting, as you had gains pretty well across the board."

Added Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co. International: "Orders are improving, inventories are still very lean and demand is still very strong. Mr. Greenspan may not like this very much, but for the economy, it's good."

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, in his semiannual economic testimony to Congress on Wednesday, credited much of the economy's recent good performance to the low rate of inflation but said that may not last. He added that the Fed had to remain vigilant.

The inflation-sensitive 30-year Treasury bond fell a quarter of a point, or $2.50 per $1,000 face value, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, rose to 6.79 percent from 6.77 percent Wednesday.

The sharpest gain in any single durable goods category last month was for electronic and electrical equipment, up 14.9 percent to $27.7 billion after drops of 14.1 percent in December and 10.3 percent in November.

The department said that it was primarily communications and electronic components that accounted for the surge in the category. Analysts said beforehand that computer demand was steady but noted communications equipment orders often occur in irregular, high-value batches.
Nearly every category of goods posted higher orders in January.

Orders for transportation equipment, the highest-value category, increased 1.2 percent to $42 billion following a 0.9 percent fall in December. The department said more demand for new cars and parts and for commercial aircraft offset weaker orders for ships and military tanks.
Excluding transportation, durable goods orders rose in January by 4.4 percent -- the biggest monthly gain since an identical rise in January 1995.
The only type of durable good for which demand fell in January was defence items, down 23.7 percent to $6.2 billion after falling 8.0 percent in December.
Orders for primary metals increased in January by 5.5 percent to $16 billion, following a 4.9 percent rise in December.

The strong January orders report suggested a positive outlook for the manufacturing sector at the beginning of 1997. Shipments of finished products also were higher than in December and backlogs of unfilled orders increased.
